passage:
Dear Pranav,

As you take over the robotics club next term, I wanted to write down what I wish someone had told me.

The first-years will be nervous. Remember how you hid behind the soldering table your first week? Give them one small job on day one so they feel part of it.

Don't fix their code for them. Sit next to them and ask what they think is wrong. It's slower, but they'll learn.

Keep the Saturday open lab going. That's where the club became a family for me, and that's why I stayed four years.

The budget file is in the shared folder. The lab keys are with the office. Please ask the college for a bigger room; we've outgrown this one.

I'll still come by to annoy you. 😄

Thomas

qa.q: Where is the budget file kept?
qa.a: In the shared folder.

qa.q: Why does Thomas care so much about how Pranav leads the club?
qa.a: Thomas loved the club and wants it to stay a welcoming place for others, as it was for Thomas.

qa.q: Which of Thomas's tips would help most with nervous first-years, and why?
qa.a: Giving them one small job on day one, because it helps them feel useful and part of the team right away.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Pranav is likely to feel trusted and encouraged, and maybe a little nervous about the responsibility.

grounding: A final-year student writes to a junior, mentoring them and handing over a club to keep the community going.

passage: Reena tucked her hair behind her ear. "So Mehak, you know how our colony's little kids just roam the lanes after school? Last year I started a Sunday reading circle in the community hall. Just me, some old storybooks from my shelf and three kids. I almost gave up after the second week, when only one came. But I kept going. Now there are fifteen, and two college friends help. The best part? Last month a Class 5 girl, who wouldn't speak at all at first, read a whole page out loud. Everyone clapped. I had to pretend I had dust in my eye. I want it to keep going after I graduate, so I'm training a Class 11 girl from our building to take over. It's not big. But it's ours."

qa.q: Where does Reena hold the Sunday reading circle?
qa.a: In the community hall.

qa.q: Why did Reena pretend she had dust in her eye?
qa.a: She was moved to tears watching the shy girl read aloud, because it showed how much the circle mattered.

qa.q: What small step shows that Reena is thinking about the future of the circle?
qa.a: Training a Class 11 girl to take over, so the circle continues even after she graduates.

qa.q: How might the Class 5 girl feel after reading aloud to applause?
qa.a: She probably felt proud and more confident, perhaps for the first time in front of a group.

grounding: A young adult describes building a small community reading circle and preparing a younger person to carry it on.

passage: Seema is in her third year, and I'm her roommate, Nandini. Every June, when the new first-years arrive at our hostel, she transforms. She waits by the gate with a notebook listing where the mess, the photocopy shop and the nearest medical store are. When a girl from Assam cried her first night, Seema sat with her on the stairs for an hour, talking about nothing in particular. She has started a "senior buddy" system, just names on a paper chart in the common room, pairing each first-year with a senior. The warden now asks her advice before making new rules. I once asked why she bothers. She said, "Someone did it for me." I don't know if that's all of it. But the hostel feels different because of her.

qa.q: What did Seema list in her notebook for new students?
qa.a: Where the mess, the photocopy shop and the nearest medical store are.

qa.q: What does Seema's reply 'Someone did it for me' suggest about her motives?
qa.a: She feels grateful for help she received and wants to pass it on, though Nandini senses there may be more to it.

qa.q: How could the warden support Seema's buddy system?
qa.a: By recognising it officially and helping pass it on to the next seniors, so it doesn't depend on one person.

qa.q: How does Nandini see her roommate's effort?
qa.a: She seems to admire her, noticing how the whole hostel has changed, even if she doesn't fully understand why Seema does it.

grounding: A roommate describes a young adult mentoring newcomers and making the hostel community more stable.

passage:
First week of term: Payal, twenty-two and in her final year, noticed a first-year, Pallavi, sitting alone at the back of the robotics club, too scared to touch the kit. Payal remembered being exactly that girl. She pulled up a chair. 'Want to break something with me?'
Mid-term: Pallavi was wiring motors on her own now and asking questions loudly. Payal started a Saturday session for first-years only, so the shy ones had space, and persuaded the club to keep a spare-parts box nobody needed permission to use.
Farewell week: Payal handed Pallavi the club's cupboard key. 'You run Saturdays now.' Pallavi's eyes widened. 'Me?' 'You. Find the next one sitting at the back.'

qa.q: What did Payal hand Pallavi in farewell week?
qa.a: The club's cupboard key.

qa.q: Why did Payal pull up a chair next to Pallavi?
qa.a: She recognised her own past fear in Pallavi and wanted to give her the welcome she once needed.

qa.q: What made Payal's mentoring last beyond her own time?
qa.a: She set up a regular session and a spare-parts box, and handed leadership to Pallavi to carry on.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt when she got the key?
qa.a: Surprised and a little nervous, but trusted and proud to pass the help on. 😊

grounding: Shows a young adult mentoring a junior and building club structures that outlast her.

passage: 'Sarita, you ask why I still go to the community hall every Sunday,' said Tejas Uncle, polishing his glasses. 'When I was twenty-one, just out of college, our basti had no place for children to study. Kids did homework under the streetlight. So a few of us cleaned out the old ration storeroom, begged tables from the temple committee, and I taught maths there every evening after work. The older kids I taught started teaching the younger ones. Some of those children are teachers now. One is the ward councillor. I was tired all the time, and some months I wanted to quit. But I learned something: a place lasts longer than one person. Build the place, beta, and let others fill it.'

qa.q: Where did the children do homework before the study room?
qa.a: Under the streetlight.

qa.q: What does 'some months I wanted to quit' show about how young Tejas felt?
qa.a: It shows the work was exhausting and he felt tempted to stop, which makes his staying more meaningful.

qa.q: What lesson could Sarita apply to Sarita's own community work?
qa.a: Build something shared, like a place or routine, and let others take it on, so it doesn't depend on one person.

qa.q: How might the children who studied there see the hall now?
qa.a: As a place that shaped their lives, which is why some became teachers and helped others.

grounding: Illustrates an elder's memory of building a lasting study space for his community as a young adult.

passage:
The power went at five, just as Rajni's Sunday maths class for the lane's children began, and the rain found every crack in the community hall roof. Nine kids stood holding their notebooks above their heads.
Rajni didn't cancel. She moved everyone to the dry verandah of the temple next door, lit two candles in steel glasses and split the group. The little ones counted beans. The older ones worked fractions on slates.
Shankar, thirteen, sat apart, as he had for weeks, pretending he'd finished.
“Shankar, I need a second teacher tonight,” Rajni said. “Can you take the bean table?”
He hesitated, then sat with the six-year-olds, and when one of them got the sum right he laughed out loud. Walking home under one umbrella, he asked if he could help next Sunday too.

qa.q: Where did Rajni move the class when the rain came in?
qa.a: She moved everyone to the dry verandah of the temple next door.

qa.q: Why might Shankar have been sitting apart for weeks?
qa.a: He was probably embarrassed that he was struggling and hid it by pretending he had finished the work.

qa.q: What made Rajni's request to Shankar a wise move?
qa.a: Giving him a real job made him feel useful instead of behind, and teaching the little ones helped him re-join the class.

qa.q: How might the six-year-olds at the bean table see Shankar?
qa.a: They see an older boy who is patient with them, which makes the sums feel less scary and more like a game 🙂

grounding: A young woman keeps her free community class going in a storm and turns a struggling boy into a helper.

passage:
On the first day of the coding club, Yash sat at the back of the lab in his new college T-shirt, laptop closed. Jasleen, a final-year student, noticed him leave early three weeks in a row.
She found him at the canteen. “Stuck?”
“Everyone already knows everything,” he muttered.
“I didn't, in first year. I cried over a missing bracket once.” She opened his laptop, looked at his half-built attendance app and said, “This is good. Want to finish it for the library?”
For a month she met him every Thursday for thirty minutes. Then she did something bigger: she started a help desk run by seniors, two evenings a week, and put up a sign-up sheet on the club noticeboard. By December, Yash was sitting at that desk himself, helping a nervous first-year from the hostel.

qa.q: How long did Jasleen meet Yash every Thursday?
qa.a: She met him every Thursday for thirty minutes for a month.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when he said everyone already knew everything?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and out of place, comparing himself to others and thinking he did not belong.

qa.q: Why did the help desk matter more than Jasleen's own meetings with Yash?
qa.a: It meant help no longer depended on one senior, so newcomers after Yash could also find support.

qa.q: What is it like for the new first-year when Yash sits at the help desk?
qa.a: The nervous student gets help from someone who struggled recently, which may make asking feel less embarrassing.

grounding: A final-year student mentors a junior and builds a lasting help desk for the club.

passage:
“Seema-ji, you've opened this library every Saturday for eleven years. Alone?”
“Who else? The children come, the books go home, some come back.”
Kunal looked at the dusty register. “What if you fall ill? It shuts.”
“Then it shuts, beta.” Seema laughed, but she rubbed her knee.
“I've been thinking. I could take the second Saturday. My friend Farah could take the fourth. And we train two of the older kids to run the register.”
“They'll lose the books.”
“Maybe a few. We'll make a simple system. Colour stickers by age, a notebook for returns.”
Seema studied him. “Why do you care? You're finishing your degree.”
“This place is where I learned to read English. It should outlast both of us.”
She slid the register across the table. “Second Saturday, then. Nine sharp.”

qa.q: How long has Seema opened the library every Saturday?
qa.a: She has opened it every Saturday for eleven years.

qa.q: What does Seema's rubbing of her knee suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she is more worried and tired than her laugh shows, and quietly aware that the library depends on her health.

qa.q: What could help Kunal's rota plan work?
qa.a: He could start small with the stickers and the returns notebook, and check in with Seema after the first month.

qa.q: Why might Kunal care about the library more than Seema expected?
qa.a: He learned to read English there, so he feels grateful and wants to protect it for younger children.

grounding: A young man offers to share and systematise a neighbourhood library so it survives beyond one person.

passage: I'm Pradeep. In my final year, I looked after the first-years in the college robotics club. One of them, Arnab, reminded me of myself at eighteen: clever, silent, too scared to touch the tools in case he broke something. I remembered how a senior had once handed me a soldering iron and said, "Break it. We'll fix it." So I did the same. Every Saturday I stayed back two extra hours. I let Arnab make mistakes I could have fixed in a minute. It was slower. Sometimes I was frustrated. But by March, he was teaching the new kids. When I graduated, the club still ran without me, and that felt better than any prize.

qa.q: What did the senior once hand Pradeep?
qa.a: A soldering iron.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel when the club still ran without Pradeep?
qa.a: Pradeep felt proud and satisfied, better than winning any prize.

qa.q: What did Pradeep do that built the club's future?
qa.a: Stayed back on Saturdays and let Arnab learn by making mistakes, until Arnab could teach others.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt when first handed the tools?
qa.a: Arnab was probably nervous and scared of breaking something, then more confident with encouragement.

grounding: A young adult reflects on mentoring a junior in a college club so it could continue after graduation.

passage:
Internship supervisor's note. Manjula Iyer, community health NGO, Chennai. Month 4.
Vijay, twenty-one, has done more than his assigned data work. He noticed that the children of our office cleaning staff wait in the corridor after school until their parents finish. On his own initiative, he set up a Saturday homework table in the meeting room, and now four other interns take turns. He asked permission first and made a sign-up sheet. He is patient with the younger ones; I saw him explain fractions with bottle caps. I have asked the board to make it an official programme with a small budget, and I've invited Vijay to write a short plan so it continues after his internship ends.

qa.q: What did Vijay use to explain fractions?
qa.a: Bottle caps.

qa.q: What might Vijay have been feeling when he noticed the children waiting in the corridor?
qa.a: He likely felt concerned and caring, wanting to help them use the time well.

qa.q: What did Manjula Iyer do to make the effort last?
qa.a: She asked the board to make it an official programme and invited Vijay to write a plan so it continues.

qa.q: How might the cleaning staff feel about the homework table?
qa.a: They may feel grateful and reassured that their children are cared for while they finish work.

grounding: A supervisor's note records a young intern building a homework programme for staff children.

passage:
Sunday. Dilnaz's diary.
The mohalla library opened today! Well, "library" = two steel almirahs in Ganga Aunty's verandah, 212 donated books, and a notebook for borrowing. I've been planning since January. Ganga Aunty gave the space; I collected books from everyone who'd listen. This morning eleven kids came. One tiny boy, Irshad, sat reading a picture book for an hour and wouldn't leave. I got teary. When I was little, there was nothing like this near us. I want it to last, not just be my project. So I've asked three older girls from the lane to be "librarians," with badges and everything. Next month, we'll ask the corporator for a proper room.

qa.q: How many books were donated?
How did Dilnaz feel watching Irshad read for an hour?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt moved and teary, happy to give children something missing from Dilnaz's own childhood.

qa.q: What is Dilnaz doing to make the library last?
qa.a: Training three older girls as librarians and planning to ask the corporator for a proper room.

qa.q: How might Ganga Aunty feel about the library in her verandah?
qa.a: Ganga Aunty likely feels proud and glad to have given the space for the children.

grounding: A young adult's diary records starting a neighbourhood library and building it to outlast its founder.

passage:
Yash had grown up in the village and was now in his final year of agriculture college. During the summer he came home and found the village library locked. The old librarian had retired; nobody had taken over.
He could have ignored it. Instead he got the key from the sarpanch and spent a week cleaning. His neighbour Seema, who was in Class 12, helped sort the books.
He set up a timetable: library open three evenings a week, older students helping younger ones with homework. Seema would run it when he went back.
On the last evening before he left, eleven children sat on mats reading. Seema asked, "What if I can't manage?"
Yash said, "You will. And I'll call every Sunday."

qa.q: How many evenings a week would the library open?
qa.a: Three evenings a week.

qa.q: What might Seema be feeling when she asks "What if I can't manage?"
qa.a: She likely feels nervous and unsure, worried about running the library alone.

qa.q: What did Yash do to make sure the library would last?
qa.a: He set up a timetable, involved older students, and handed it to Seema with weekly calls for support.

qa.q: How might the children in the village see the reopened library?
qa.a: They may feel happy and excited to have a place to read and get help with homework.

grounding: Shows a young adult building a lasting community space and mentoring a younger person.

passage:
Emil joined the Berlin community swimming club as a boy, and now, at twenty, he coached the beginners on Wednesday evenings.
This season a new girl, Zeynep, came with her mother. She was eleven, newly arrived, and afraid of putting her face in the water.
Emil didn't push. Each week he gave her one small step: blowing bubbles, then floating with a board, then kicking to the wall. He also started pairing the older teens with beginners, so the club wasn't relying only on him.
By December Zeynep swam a full length. The older teens cheered louder than the parents.
Afterwards the club manager asked Emil if he'd join the committee. He hesitated, then said yes. "Someone did this for me once."

qa.q: What did Emil give Zeynep each week?
qa.a: One small step: blowing bubbles, then floating with a board, then kicking to the wall.

qa.q: How was Zeynep feeling at the start of the season?
qa.a: She was afraid of putting her face in the water, anxious in a new place.

qa.q: How did Emil make the club stronger, not just Zeynep's swimming?
qa.a: He paired older teens with beginners so the club wouldn't rely on him alone, and later joined the committee.

qa.q: What is it like for the older teens when Zeynep swims a full length?
qa.a: They feel proud and involved, cheering louder than the parents.

grounding: Shows a young adult mentoring children and strengthening his community club.

passage:
The coding club room in the hostel basement smelled of instant noodles and old carpet. Ojas, a third-year, noticed the new first-year in the corner, Tanvir, staring at a red error message for twenty minutes without asking anyone.
"Mind if I sit?" Ojas pulled a chair over. "That error ate my whole first month too."
Tanvir shrugged. "I don't want to waste your time."
"You're not. Seniors did this for me." Ojas didn't touch the keyboard. "Read the last line out loud. What do you think it's complaining about?"
Tanvir read it, frowned, then found the missing bracket himself. He grinned for the first time that evening.
Later Ojas wrote on the club whiteboard: "Stuck for 15 minutes? Ask a senior. Tuesdays and Thursdays, 7 pm." Below it he listed three names, his own first, and asked two other seniors to add theirs.

qa.q: What did Ojas write on the club whiteboard?
qa.a: He wrote "Stuck for 15 minutes? Ask a senior. Tuesdays and Thursdays, 7 pm."

qa.q: Why did Tanvir avoid asking for help at first?
qa.a: He was embarrassed and worried he would waste a senior's time, so he stayed stuck alone for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Ojas do well as a mentor?
qa.a: He let Tanvir find the bug himself instead of taking the keyboard, and then turned one helpful moment into a regular system other seniors could join.

qa.q: What is it like for Tanvir when a senior sits beside him and says the error ate his whole first month too?
qa.a: It likely makes Tanvir feel less alone and less foolish, which makes it easier for him to try again and grin at his own fix.

grounding: Shows a young adult mentoring a younger peer and setting up a lasting structure in a student organisation.
